A transfer experiment on 500 IGLU collaborative building tasks confirm the effect generalizes beyond the primary benchmark.

AI.tldr: A neuro-symbolic pipeline using 2.5-D decomposition (LLM plans in 2D, deterministic executor handles vertical placement) achieves 94.6% accuracy on block-building tasks, outperforming standard LLM approaches by eliminating coordinate errors, and transfers directly to edge hardware.
AI.motivation: LLMs make systematic coordinate errors in 3D spatial reasoning when generating block placements from natural-language instructions, limiting their reliability for autonomous construction tasks.
AI.method: 2.5-D decomposition: the LLM plans only in the 2D horizontal plane while a deterministic executor computes vertical placement from column occupancy, removing the third dimension from the LLM's output space.
AI.result: 94.6% mean structural accuracy on the Build What I Mean benchmark (160 rounds, 12 runs), within 3.0 percentage points of the 97.6% ceiling; outperforms GPT-4o (90.3%) and best competing system (76.3%); ablation shows 2.5-D decomposition contributes 50.7 percentage points; transfers to edge hardware at 94.5% with no prompt modifications.
AI.conclusion: Removing deterministic dimensions from the LLM's output space is an effective principle for spatial reasoning in autonomous construction, generalizable to any task where physical constraints fix degrees of freedom.

title: TAVIS: A Benchmark for Egocentric Active Vision and Anticipatory Gaze in Imitation Learning
summary: Active vision -- where a policy controls its own gaze during manipulation -- has emerged as a key capability for imitation learning, with multiple independent systems demonstrating its benefits in the past year. Yet there is no shared benchmark to compare approaches or quantify what active vision contributes, on which task types, and under what conditions. We introduce TAVIS, evaluation infrastructure for active-vision imitation learning, with two complementary task suites -- TAVIS-Head (5 tasks, global search via pan/tilt necks) and TAVIS-Hands (3 tasks, local occlusion via wrist cameras) -- on two humanoid torso embodiments (GR1T2, Reachy2), built on IsaacLab. TAVIS provides three evaluation primitives: a paired headcam-vs-fixedcam protocol on identical demonstrations; GALT (Gaze-Action Lead Time), a novel metric grounded in cognitive science and HRI that quantifies anticipatory gaze in learned policies; and procedural ID/OOD splits. Baseline experiments with Diffusion Policy and $π_0$ reveal that (i) active-vision generally helps, but benefits are task-conditional rather than uniform; (ii) multi-task policies degrade sharply under controlled distribution shifts on both suites; and (iii) imitation alone yields anticipatory gaze, with median lead times comparable to the human teleoperator reference. Code, evaluation scripts, demonstrations (LeRobot v3.0; ~2200 episodes) and trained baselines are released at https://github.com/spiglerg/tavis and https://huggingface.co/tavis-benchmark.

AI.tldr: TAVIS is a standardized benchmark for evaluating active-vision imitation learning, consisting of 8 tasks across two humanoid embodiments, with a paired headcam-vs-fixedcam protocol, a novel anticipatory gaze metric (GALT), and procedural ID/OOD splits. Experiments show active-vision benefits are task-conditional, multi-task policies degrade under distribution shifts, and imitation alone produces anticipatory gaze comparable to human teleoperators.
AI.motivation: Despite multiple active-vision imitation learning systems emerging, there is no shared benchmark to compare approaches, quantify what active vision contributes, on which task types, and under what conditions.
AI.method: TAVIS provides: (1) two task suites (TAVIS-Head: 5 tasks with pan/tilt necks for global search; TAVIS-Hands: 3 tasks with wrist cameras for local occlusion) on GR1T2 and Reachy2 humanoid embodiments built on IsaacLab; (2) three evaluation primitives — paired headcam-vs-fixedcam protocol on identical demonstrations, GALT (Gaze-Action Lead Time) metric for anticipatory gaze quantification, and procedural ID/OOD splits; (3) baseline experiments with Diffusion Policy and π₀.
AI.result: Active-vision generally helps but benefits are task-conditional rather than uniform; multi-task policies degrade sharply under controlled distribution shifts; imitation alone yields anticipatory gaze with median lead times comparable to human teleoperator reference.
AI.conclusion: TAVIS establishes a standardized evaluation infrastructure for active-vision imitation learning, enabling fair comparison of approaches and revealing nuanced insights about when and how active vision helps.

title: TeamBench: Evaluating Agent Coordination under Enforced Role Separation
summary: Agent systems often decompose a task across multiple roles, but these roles are typically specified by prompts rather than enforced by access controls. Without enforcement, a team pass rate can mask whether agents actually coordinated or whether one role effectively did another role's work. We present TeamBench, a benchmark with 851 task templates and 931 seeded instances for evaluating agent coordination under operating system-enforced role separation. TeamBench separates specification access, workspace editing, and final certification across Planner, Executor, and Verifier roles, so that no role can read the full requirements, modify the workspace, and certify the final answer. Prompt-only and sandbox-enforced teams reach statistically indistinguishable pass rates, but prompt-only runs produce 3.6 times more cases where the verifier attempts to edit the executor's code. Verifiers approve 49% of submissions that fail the deterministic grader, and removing the verifier improves mean partial score in the ablation. Team value is also conditional. Teams benefit when single agents struggle, but hurt when single agents already perform well. A 40-session human study under the same role separation shows that our benchmark exposes interaction patterns that pass rate misses. Solo participants work through the task directly, human participants paired with agents often collapse into quick approval, and human teams spend more effort coordinating missing information across roles.

AI.tldr: TeamBench is a benchmark with 851 task templates and 931 seeded instances that evaluates agent coordination under OS-enforced role separation across Planner, Executor, and Verifier roles. Prompt-only teams show similar pass rates to sandbox-enforced teams but produce 3.6× more cases where verifiers attempt editing executor code. Verifiers approve 49% of submissions that fail the grader, and teams help when single agents struggle but hurt when single agents already perform well. A 40-session human study reveals coordination patterns that pass rate alone misses.
AI.motivation: Agent systems often decompose tasks across multiple roles specified by prompts without access control enforcement, allowing a team pass rate to mask whether agents actually coordinated or whether one role effectively did another role's work.
AI.method: TeamBench enforces operating system-level role separation with three roles—Planner (specification access), Executor (workspace editing), and Verifier (final certification)—such that no single role can read full requirements, modify the workspace, and certify answers. The benchmark includes 851 task templates and 931 seeded instances, and was evaluated through both automated testing and a 40-session human study.
AI.result: Prompt-only and sandbox-enforced teams achieve statistically indistinguishable pass rates, but prompt-only runs produce 3.6× more cases where verifiers attempt editing executor code. Verifiers approve 49% of submissions failing the deterministic grader. Removing the verifier improves mean partial score in ablation. Team value is conditional: beneficial when single agents struggle, detrimental when single agents perform well.
AI.conclusion: Role separation enforced at the OS level reveals coordination failures that pass rate obscures, and simple benchmark metrics like pass rate can be misleading for evaluating multi-agent systems. Human studies further confirm that different coordination patterns emerge under enforced role separation.

title: Evaluation of an Actuated Spine in Agile Quadruped Locomotion
summary: The spine plays a crucial role in the dynamic locomotion of quadrupedal animals, improving the stability, speed, and efficiency of their gait, especially for fast-paced and highly agile movements. Therefore, the spine is also a promising and natural way to extend the capabilities of quadruped robots. This paper empirically investigates the benefits of an actuated spine for learning agile quadruped locomotion. We evaluate whether the use of the spine brings benefits in terms of high-speed running, climbing stairs, climbing high-angle slopes, hurdling, and crawling scenarios. We conducted an empirical study in MuJoCo simulation using the Silver Badger robot from MAB Robotics with an actuated 1-DOF spine in the sagittal plane. The obtained results show that the use of the spine provides the robot with increased agility and allows it to overcome higher stairs, steeper slopes, higher obstacles, and smaller passages.

AI.tldr: This paper empirically investigates the benefits of an actuated 1-DOF spine (sagittal plane) for quadruped robot locomotion in MuJoCo simulation using the Silver Badger robot, finding that the spine improves agility, speed, stair climbing, slope climbing, hurdling, and crawling capabilities.
AI.motivation: The spine is crucial for dynamic locomotion in quadrupedal animals (stability, speed, efficiency) and is a promising natural way to extend quadruped robot capabilities, but lacks empirical investigation in learning-based agile locomotion.
AI.method: Empirical study in MuJoCo simulation using the Silver Badger robot from MAB Robotics with an actuated 1-DOF spine in the sagittal plane, evaluating high-speed running, stair climbing, high-angle slope climbing, hurdling, and crawling scenarios.
AI.result: The actuated spine provides increased agility, allowing the robot to overcome higher stairs, steeper slopes, higher obstacles, and smaller passages.
AI.conclusion: An actuated spine benefits agile quadruped locomotion across multiple challenging scenarios, enhancing performance beyond what is achievable without spinal actuation.

title: Online Allocation with Unknown Shared Supply
summary: Many real-world resource allocation systems, such as humanitarian logistics and vaccine distribution, must preposition limited supply across multiple locations before demand is realized while stockouts incur irreversible service losses. To study this, we introduce the Online Shared Supply Allocation (OSSA) problem, a stateful online model in which a central hub allocates a finite, unknown supply to multiple sites facing sequential demand under fixed-charge transportation costs and lost-sales penalties. Unlike classical make-to-stock or make-to-order inventory models, OSSA precludes backlogging and replenishment only hedges against future demand. To tackle OSSA, we propose a deterministic threshold-proportional policy GPA and prove that it achieves a $4/3$-approximation to the offline optimum up to an additive term independent of the total supply. We complement this with matching lower bounds showing that the $4/3$ ratio is tight and that the additive-error dependence is unavoidable, even for randomized algorithms that know the total supply upfront. Finally, we develop a learning-augmented extension to GPA that principally incorporates imperfect forecasts (e.g., from human experts or ML models) commonly available in practice, enabling us to exploit high-quality advice while being robust against arbitrary bad ones. Synthetic and real-world experiments show that GPA outperforms natural baselines with global supply is scarce.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Online Shared Supply Allocation (OSSA) problem for prepositioning limited supply across multiple locations before demand is realized, proposes a deterministic threshold-proportional policy (GPA) with a tight $4/3$-approximation to the offline optimum, and extends it with a learning-augmented variant that robustly incorporates imperfect forecasts.
AI.motivation: Real-world resource allocation systems (e.g., humanitarian logistics, vaccine distribution) must preposition limited supply across multiple locations before demand is known, where stockouts cause irreversible service losses. Existing inventory models (make-to-stock/make-to-order) do not capture this stateful online allocation under fixed-charge transportation costs and lost-sales penalties.
AI.method: The paper models the OSSA problem as a stateful online model where a central hub allocates finite, unknown supply to multiple sites facing sequential demand. It proposes a deterministic threshold-proportional policy (GPA) and proves a $4/3$-approximation to the offline optimum (up to an additive term). It also develops a learning-augmented extension that integrates imperfect forecasts (human/ML) with robustness guarantees.
AI.result: GPA achieves a $4/3$-approximation to the offline optimum up to an additive term independent of total supply. Matching lower bounds show the $4/3$ ratio is tight and the additive-error dependence is unavoidable, even for randomized algorithms knowing total supply upfront. Experiments show GPA outperforms natural baselines when global supply is scarce.
AI.conclusion: The GPA policy provides a theoretically tight approximation for the OSSA problem, and its learning-augmented extension enables practical deployment by exploiting high-quality advice while remaining robust against poor forecasts.

title: Active Embodiment Identification with Reinforcement Learning for Legged Robots
summary: We present an active embodiment identification method for legged robots that jointly learns information-seeking behavior and explicit embodiment prediction. Using a history-augmented URMA architecture, the method infers joint-level and global embodiment parameters through interaction with the environment in simulation across different morphologies.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an active embodiment identification method for legged robots that jointly learns information-seeking behavior and explicit embodiment prediction using a history-augmented URMA architecture.
AI.motivation: To enable legged robots to autonomously identify their own embodiment parameters (joint-level and global) through active interaction with the environment, without prior knowledge of their morphology.
AI.method: A history-augmented URMA (Universal Robot Morphology Architecture) is used to jointly learn information-seeking behaviors and explicit embodiment prediction. The method operates in simulation across different morphologies, inferring both joint-level and global embodiment parameters through interaction.
AI.result: The method successfully infers joint-level and global embodiment parameters across different morphologies by actively interacting with the environment in simulation.
AI.conclusion: The proposed active embodiment identification approach enables legged robots to autonomously discover their own body configuration through purposeful interaction, which is essential for adaptation and control in unknown or changing physical conditions.

title: ARMOR: An Agentic Framework for Reaction Feasibility Prediction via Adaptive Utility-aware Multi-tool Reasoning
summary: Reaction feasibility prediction, as a fundamental problem in computational chemistry, has benefited from diverse tools enabled by recent advances in artificial intelligence, particularly large language models. However, the performance of individual tools varies substantially across reactions, making it difficult for any single tool to consistently perform well across all cases. This raises a critical challenge: how to effectively leverage multiple tools to obtain more accurate feasibility predictions. To address this, we propose ARMOR, an agentic framework that explicitly models tool-specific utilities, adaptively prioritizes tools, and further resolves the potential tool conflicts to produce the final prediction for each reaction. Unlike existing approaches that rely on simple aggregation or heuristic assignment over various tools, ARMOR organizes tools into a hierarchy that prioritizes top-performing tools and defers others when needed, characterizes their strengths through tool-specific patterns, and resolves conflicts via memoryaugmented reasoning. Extensive experiments on a public dataset demonstrate that ARMOR consistently outperforms strong baselines, including single-tool methods as well as various tool aggregation and tool selection approaches. Further analysis shows that the improvements are particularly significant on reactions with conflicting tool predictions, highlighting the effectiveness of ARMOR in leveraging the complementary strengths of multiple tools. The code is available via https://anonymous.4open.science/r/ARMOR-E13F.

AI.tldr: ARMOR is an agentic framework that improves reaction feasibility prediction by explicitly modeling tool-specific utilities, adaptively prioritizing tools, and resolving conflicts among multiple prediction tools through hierarchical organization and memory-augmented reasoning.
AI.motivation: Individual prediction tools for reaction feasibility vary substantially in performance across different reactions, and no single tool consistently performs well. The challenge is how to effectively leverage multiple tools to obtain more accurate and robust feasibility predictions.
AI.method: ARMOR organizes tools into a hierarchy that prioritizes top-performing tools and defers others when needed, characterizes their strengths through tool-specific patterns, and resolves conflicts via memory-augmented reasoning to produce final predictions.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on a public dataset show ARMOR consistently outperforms strong baselines including single-tool methods, tool aggregation, and tool selection approaches. Improvements are particularly significant on reactions with conflicting tool predictions.
AI.conclusion: ARMOR effectively leverages the complementary strengths of multiple tools to produce more accurate reaction feasibility predictions, especially in challenging cases where individual tools disagree.

title: 123D: Unifying Multi-Modal Autonomous Driving Data at Scale
summary: The pursuit of autonomous driving has produced one of the richest sensor data collections in all of robotics. However, its scale and diversity remain largely untapped. Each dataset adopts different 2D and 3D modalities, such as cameras, lidar, ego states, annotations, traffic lights, and HD maps, with different rates and synchronization schemes. They come in fragmented formats requiring complex dependencies that cannot natively coexist in the same development environment. Further, major inconsistencies in annotation conventions prevent training or measuring generalization across multiple datasets. We present 123D, an open-source framework that unifies such multi-modal driving data through a single API. To handle synchronization, we store each modality as an independent timestamped event stream with no prescribed rate, enabling synchronous or asynchronous access across arbitrary datasets. Using 123D, we consolidate eight real-world driving datasets spanning 3,300 hours and 90,000 kilometers, together with a synthetic dataset with configurable collection scripts, and provide tools for data analysis and visualization. We conduct a systematic study comparing annotation statistics and assessing each dataset's pose and calibration accuracy. Further, we showcase two applications 123D enables: cross-dataset 3D object detection transfer and reinforcement learning for planning, and offer recommendations for future directions. Code and documentation are available at https://github.com/kesai-labs/py123d.

AI.tldr: 123D is an open-source framework that unifies fragmented multi-modal driving datasets (8 real-world + 1 synthetic) spanning 3,300 hours and 90,000 km through a single timestamped event-stream API, enabling cross-dataset 3D detection transfer and RL planning.
AI.motivation: Existing autonomous driving datasets are fragmented across different formats, modalities, rates, annotation conventions, and dependencies, preventing them from coexisting in the same development environment and hindering cross-dataset generalization and training.
AI.method: 123D stores each sensor modality as an independent timestamped event stream with no prescribed rate, enabling synchronous or asynchronous access. It consolidates 8 real-world datasets and 1 synthetic dataset via a unified API, with tools for analysis and visualization.
AI.result: Consolidated 3,300 hours and 90,000 km of driving data; systematic comparison of annotation statistics, pose/calibration accuracy; demonstrated cross-dataset 3D object detection transfer and reinforcement learning for planning.
AI.conclusion: 123D enables unified multi-modal driving data access and cross-dataset applications, with recommendations for future dataset and framework directions.

title: Switchcraft: AI Model Router for Agentic Tool Calling
summary: Agentic AI systems that invoke external tools are powerful but costly, leading developers to default to large models and overspend inference budgets. Model routing can mitigate this, but existing routers are designed for chat completion rather than tool use. We present Switchcraft, the first (to the best of our knowledge) model router optimized for agentic tool calling. Switchcraft operates inline, selecting the lowest-cost model subject to correctness. We construct an evaluation framework on five function-calling benchmarks and train a DistilBERT-based classifier, deployed under a latency budget. Switchcraft achieves 82.9% accuracy -- matching or exceeding the best individual model -- while reducing inference cost by 84%, saving over $3,600 per million queries. We find that larger models do not consistently outperform smaller ones on tool-use tasks, and that nominally cheaper models can incur higher total cost due to token-intensive reasoning. Our work enables cost-aware agentic AI deployment without sacrificing correctness.

AI.tldr: Switchcraft is a model router optimized for agentic tool calling that selects the lowest-cost correct model, achieving 82.9% accuracy (matching best individual models) while reducing inference cost by 84% ($3,600 savings per million queries).
AI.motivation: Agentic AI systems that invoke external tools are costly, and developers default to large models overspending inference budgets. Existing routers are designed for chat completion rather than tool use.
AI.method: Switchcraft is a DistilBERT-based classifier trained on five function-calling benchmarks, deployed under a latency budget, operating inline to select the lowest-cost model subject to correctness.
AI.result: Switchcraft achieves 82.9% accuracy, matches or exceeds the best individual model, reduces inference cost by 84%, and saves over $3,600 per million queries.
AI.conclusion: Larger models do not consistently outperform smaller ones on tool-use tasks; nominally cheaper models can incur higher total cost due to token-intensive reasoning. Switchcraft enables cost-aware agentic AI deployment without sacrificing correctness.

title: AdaTKG: Adaptive Memory for Temporal Knowledge Graph Reasoning
summary: Temporal knowledge graphs (TKGs) represent time-stamped relational facts and support a wide range of reasoning tasks over evolving events. However, existing methods produce entity representations that are static at the entity level, in that each representation is a function of learned parameters only and retains no trace of the interactions in which the entity has participated. In this paper, we depart from this static view and propose that each entity be modeled as an adaptive process whose representation is refined every time the entity participates in a fact. To this end, we propose AdaTKG, which maintains a per-entity memory that is updated with every observed interaction, with the memory accumulating online and predictions improving as more interactions arrive. Specifically, we instantiate the memory update as a learnable exponential moving average governed by a single shared scalar instead of using learnable parameters for each entity, enabling AdaTKG to handle entities unseen during training. Extensive experiments confirm consistent gains over TKG baselines, demonstrating the effectiveness of adaptive memory. Code is publicly available at: https://github.com/seunghan96/AdaTKG.

AI.tldr: AdaTKG models entities as adaptive processes with per-entity memory updated via learnable exponential moving average, improving TKG reasoning over static entity representations.
AI.motivation: Existing TKG methods produce static entity representations that are solely functions of learned parameters and retain no trace of the entity's past interactions, limiting reasoning over evolving events.
AI.method: AdaTKG maintains a per-entity memory updated with every observed interaction using a learnable exponential moving average governed by a single shared scalar (instead of entity-specific parameters), enabling handling of unseen entities.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show consistent gains over TKG baselines, confirming the effectiveness of adaptive memory.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive entity memory that accumulates online and refines representations upon each interaction improves TKG reasoning performance, and the approach generalizes to unseen entities.

title: Finite-Time Analysis of MCTS in Continuous POMDP Planning
summary: This paper presents a finite-time analysis for Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) in Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs), with probabilistic concentration bounds in both discrete and continuous observation spaces. While MCTS-style solvers such as POMCP achieve empirical success in many applications, rigorous finite-time guarantees remain an open problem due to the nonstationarity and the interdependencies induced by heuristic action selection (e.g., UCB). In the discrete setting, we address these challenges by extending the polynomial exploration bonus to UCB in POMDP setting, yielding polynomial concentration bounds for the empirical value estimation at the root node. For continuous observation spaces, we introduce an abstract partitioning framework and propose a finite-time bound on partitioning loss. Under mild conditions, we prove highprobability bound on value estimates in POMDPs with continuous observation space. Specifically, we propose Voro-POMCPOW, a variant of POMCPOW with f inite-time guarantees that adaptively partitions the continuous observation space using Voronoi cells. This approach maintains a finite branching factor while preserving the original observation generator. Empirical validation demonstrates that the proposed Voro-POMCPOW shows competitive performance while providing theoretical guarantees. Although our analysis focuses on continuous POMDPs, the techniques developed herein are also applicable to continuous MDPs, closing another gap on the MDP side.

AI.tldr: This paper provides finite-time theoretical guarantees for Monte Carlo Tree Search in POMDPs, introducing Voro-POMCPOW for continuous observation spaces with Voronoi-based adaptive partitioning, and proving high-probability concentration bounds for value estimation in both discrete and continuous settings.
AI.motivation: MCTS-style solvers like POMCP achieve empirical success in POMDPs, but rigorous finite-time guarantees remain open due to nonstationarity and interdependencies from heuristic action selection (e.g., UCB).
AI.method: Extends polynomial exploration bonus to UCB in discrete POMDPs; introduces an abstract partitioning framework for continuous observation spaces; proposes Voro-POMCPOW which adaptively partitions continuous observation space using Voronoi cells to maintain finite branching factor while preserving the observation generator.
AI.result: Derives polynomial concentration bounds for empirical value estimation at the root node in discrete settings; provides finite-time bounds on partitioning loss and high-probability bounds on value estimates for continuous POMDPs under mild conditions; empirical validation shows Voro-POMCPOW achieves competitive performance with theoretical guarantees.
AI.conclusion: The paper closes a theoretical gap in MCTS for POMDPs by providing finite-time guarantees; techniques developed are also applicable to continuous MDPs, addressing another gap on the MDP side.

title: Can You Break RLVER? Probing Adversarial Robustness of RL-Trained Empathetic Agents
summary: Reinforcement learning from verifiable emotion rewards RLVER has produced language models with strong empathetic performance, evaluated on benchmarks that assume cooperative, honest users. Yet real emotional interactions systematically violate this assumption: users gaslight, escalate, and pressure AI systems for unconditional validation, dynamics that cooperative benchmarks cannot surface. We construct the Adversarial Empathy Benchmark AEB and introduce the Emotional Consistency Score ECS to evaluate empathetic robustness under adversarial conditions. AEB comprises six psychologically grounded adversarial trajectory types with discriminative reward structures that penalize formulaic responses; ECS formally disentangles a model's capacity to track user emotional states from its capacity to improve them. In a controlled experiment across eight scenario-matched conditions (think and no-think conditions on 2 RLVER models, and 2 base models (Qwen 1.5B and 7B) with 480 adversarial dialogues), RLVER-PPO-Think substantially outperforms the same-scale untuned baseline (0.963 vs. 0.761, \(p<0.001, r=0.688\)), with zero dialogue collapses and 47\% higher hidden-intention detection. However, ECS remains nearly flat and is not significantly different for RLVER-PPO-Think versus Base-7B-Think (\(p=0.650\)): RL training improves emotional responsiveness without measurable gains in observable state tracking. We interpret the ECS--FS (Final Score) gap as a behavioral/legibility dissociation inside this simulator family, not as evidence about internal understanding or clinical readiness.

AI.tldr: RLVER models achieve high empathetic performance on cooperative benchmarks but fail under adversarial emotional dynamics (gaslighting, escalation, pressure). The paper introduces AEB (Adversarial Empathy Benchmark) and ECS (Emotional Consistency Score) to evaluate adversarial robustness. RLVER-PPO-Think outperforms baselines on standard metrics but shows no significant gain in emotional state tracking (ECS), revealing a behavioral/legibility dissociation.
AI.motivation: Existing empathy benchmarks assume cooperative, honest users, but real emotional interactions involve adversarial dynamics (gaslighting, escalation, pressure). The paper aims to evaluate whether RLVER models are robust to such adversarial conditions, which cooperative benchmarks cannot surface.
AI.method: Constructed the Adversarial Empathy Benchmark (AEB) with six psychologically grounded adversarial trajectory types and discriminative reward structures. Introduced Emotional Consistency Score (ECS) to disentangle emotional state tracking from emotional improvement capacity. Evaluated across eight scenario-matched conditions (think/no-think on 2 RLVER models and 2 base models (Qwen 1.5B and 7B)) with 480 adversarial dialogues.
AI.result: RLVER-PPO-Think outperformed untuned baseline (0.963 vs. 0.761, p<0.001, r=0.688) with zero dialogue collapses and 47% higher hidden-intention detection. However, ECS remained nearly flat and not significantly different from Base-7B-Think (p=0.650). RL training improved emotional responsiveness without measurable gains in observable state tracking.
AI.conclusion: The ECS–FS gap reveals a behavioral/legibility dissociation in this simulator family: models learn to produce better emotional responses without genuinely improving user emotional state tracking. This is not evidence about internal understanding or clinical readiness, but a caution about benchmark limitations in adversarial settings.

title: SREGym: A Live Benchmark for AI SRE Agents with High-Fidelity Failure Scenarios
summary: AI agents are increasingly used to diagnose and mitigate failures in production systems, known as agentic Site Reliability Engineering (SRE). Current SRE benchmarks are limited to oversimplistic SRE tasks and are unfortunately hard to extend due to bespoke designs. We present SREGym, a high-fidelity benchmark for SRE agents. SREGym exposes a live system environment built atop real-world cloud-native system stacks, where high-fidelity failure scenarios are simulated through fault injectors. SREGym models the complexity of production environments by simulating (1) a wide range of faults at different layers, (2) various ambient noises, and (3) diverse failure modes such as metastable failures and correlated failures. SREGym is architected as a modular, extensible framework that orchestrates fault and noise injectors across stacks. SREGym currently includes 90 realistic, challenging SRE problems. We use SREGym to evaluate frontier agents and show that their capabilities varies significantly in addressing different kinds of failures, with up to 40% differences in end-to-end results. SREGym is actively maintained as an open-source project and has been used by researchers and practitioners.

AI.tldr: SREGym is a high-fidelity, extensible benchmark for agentic SRE, featuring 90 realistic failure scenarios across cloud-native stacks, with fault/noise injection, revealing up to 40% performance variance among frontier agents.
AI.motivation: Current SRE benchmarks are oversimplistic, hard to extend due to bespoke designs, and fail to capture the complexity of production environments for evaluating AI agents in Site Reliability Engineering.
AI.method: SREGym builds a live system environment atop real-world cloud-native stacks, simulates multi-layer faults, ambient noises, and diverse failure modes (metastable, correlated), and uses modular orchestration of fault/noise injectors across stacks.
AI.result: Evaluated frontier agents on 90 realistic SRE problems; showed significant capability variance (up to 40% difference in end-to-end results) across different failure types.
AI.conclusion: SREGym provides a realistic, extensible benchmark for agentic SRE, revealing that current agents' performance varies substantially across failure scenarios, and is openly available as a maintained open-source project.

title: Repeated Deceptive Path Planning against Learnable Observer
comment: Full version of the extended abstract accepted at AAMAS 2026
summary: We study the problem of deceptive path planning (DPP), where an agent aims to conceal its true destination from external observers. While existing work assumes static, non-learning observers, real-world adversaries-such as in critical goods transportation or military operations-can adapt by learning from historical trajectories. To address this gap, we introduce Repeated Deceptive Path Planning (RDPP), a new formulation that explicitly models learnable observers. We show that existing DPP methods fail under this setting, as they cannot adapt to evolving adversarial predictions. While incorporating observer previous predictions into updates enables some adaptation, such incremental updates cause accumulative lag that degrades deception. To this end, we propose Deceptive Meta Planning (DeMP), a two-level optimization framework that combines episode-level adaptation, which enables short-term policy adjustment to counter updated observer, and meta-level updates, which leverage cross-episode feedback to capture how observers update their models and accelerate adaptation in future episodes. In this way, DeMP mitigates the accumulation of adaptation lag, enabling sustained deception against a learning observer. Experiments across environments demonstrate that DeMP significantly outperforms existing approaches in RDPP while maintaining competitive path cost. Our results highlight the importance of modeling repeated interactions with learnable adversaries, providing new insights into deception and privacy in multi-agent systems.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Repeated Deceptive Path Planning (RDPP) to model learnable observers who adapt from historical trajectories, and proposes Deceptive Meta Planning (DeMP)—a two-level optimization framework combining episode-level adaptation and meta-level updates—to enable sustained deception against learning adversaries, outperforming existing methods.
AI.motivation: Existing deceptive path planning (DPP) methods assume static, non-learning observers, which fails to model real-world adversaries (e.g., in military or logistics) that can learn from historical trajectories and adapt their predictions over time.
AI.method: Deceptive Meta Planning (DeMP) is a two-level optimization framework: (1) episode-level adaptation for short-term policy adjustment against an updated observer, and (2) meta-level updates leveraging cross-episode feedback to capture how observers update their models and accelerate future adaptation, thereby mitigating accumulative adaptation lag.
AI.result: DeMP significantly outperforms existing DPP approaches under the RDPP setting across multiple environments while maintaining competitive path cost.
AI.conclusion: Modeling repeated interactions with learnable adversaries is crucial for sustained deception; DeMP provides new insights into deception and privacy in multi-agent systems.

title: Three-in-One World Model: Energy-Based Consistency, Prediction, and Counterfactual Inference for Marketing Intervention
summary: Marketing decisions reflect the interaction of latent consumer heterogeneity, time-varying internal states, and explicit interventions, a structure that current prediction- and language-oriented models do not capture in a unified manner. We propose a Three-in-One world-model architecture in which a Deep Boltzmann Machine (DBM) learns a frozen belief representation from demographics, time, and lagged actions and outcomes, with lightweight task-specific adapters attached on top. The same belief supports three tasks within a single framework: (i) energy-based consistency evaluation through the DBM's free energy, (ii) outcome prediction through adapters, and (iii) counterfactual inference by holding the belief fixed and varying only the action input given to the adapter. Using a controlled simulation in which the latent price sensitivity, promotion responsiveness, and base preference of each consumer are known, we show that the adapters match a strong MLP baseline on visit- and purchase-AUC while recovering heterogeneous treatment effects substantially better than S-, T-, X-, and DR-learner meta-learners and a Causal Forest baseline built on the same raw features, with the largest gap on a confounded price-promotion intervention. Complementing this, free-energy clamps systematically penalize counterfactual purchase trajectories that lack prior promotional exposure, and the penalty itself depends on the latent base preference in the expected direction. These results indicate that DBM beliefs disentangle latent traits in a form that survives counterfactual queries, providing an integrated world-model substrate for marketing intervention.

AI.tldr: Proposes a Three-in-One world-model (DBM + adapters) that unifies consistency evaluation, outcome prediction, and counterfactual inference for marketing decisions, outperforming meta-learners on heterogeneous treatment effect recovery while matching MLP baselines on prediction AUC.
AI.motivation: Marketing decisions involve latent consumer heterogeneity, time-varying states, and explicit interventions, but existing prediction- and language-oriented models do not capture this structure in a unified manner.
AI.method: A DBM learns a frozen belief representation from demographics, time, and lagged actions/outcomes; lightweight task-specific adapters are attached on top. The same belief supports energy-based consistency evaluation, outcome prediction, and counterfactual inference (by fixing belief and varying action input).
AI.result: Adapters match a strong MLP baseline on visit- and purchase-AUC while recovering heterogeneous treatment effects substantially better than S-, T-, X-, DR-learners and Causal Forest. Free-energy clamps systematically penalize counterfactual purchase trajectories lacking prior promotional exposure, with penalty depending on latent base preference as expected.
AI.conclusion: DBM beliefs disentangle latent traits in a form that survives counterfactual queries, providing an integrated world-model substrate for marketing intervention.

title: Towards Autonomous Business Intelligence via Data-to-Insight Discovery Agent
summary: Transforming fragmented enterprise data into actionable insights remains a significant challenge for LLMs, constrained by complex database schemas, limitations in dynamic SQL generation, and the need for deep multi-dimensional analysis.In this paper, we propose AIDA(Autonomous Insight Discovery Agent), the first end-to-end framework designed for autonomous exploration in complex business environments. We establish a highly flexible instant retail environment encompassing 200+ metrics and 100+ dimensions, and integrates a proprietary Domain-Specific Language (DSL) that bridges semantic reasoning with precise SQL execution. Our reinforcement learning system subsequently formulates business analysis as a Pareto Principle-guided cumulative reasoning process. Experimental results demonstrate that AIDA significantly outperforms workflow-based agents, and extensive evaluations further reveal that AIDA achieves superior environmental perception and more in-depth analysis from diverse perspectives. Our work ultimately establishes the transformative potential of autonomous intelligence for industrial-scale business intelligence systems.

AI.tldr: AIDA is an end-to-end autonomous framework that uses reinforcement learning and a domain-specific language to transform fragmented enterprise data into actionable insights, significantly outperforming workflow-based agents in complex business environments with 200+ metrics and 100+ dimensions.
AI.motivation: Transforming fragmented enterprise data into actionable insights remains a significant challenge for LLMs due to complex database schemas, limitations in dynamic SQL generation, and the need for deep multi-dimensional analysis.
AI.method: AIDA integrates a proprietary Domain-Specific Language (DSL) bridging semantic reasoning with precise SQL execution, and employs a reinforcement learning system that formulates business analysis as a Pareto Principle-guided cumulative reasoning process.
AI.result: AIDA significantly outperforms workflow-based agents, achieving superior environmental perception and more in-depth analysis from diverse perspectives in an instant retail environment with 200+ metrics and 100+ dimensions.
AI.conclusion: Autonomous intelligence has transformative potential for industrial-scale business intelligence systems.

title: HMACE: Heterogeneous Multi-Agent Collaborative Evolution for Combinatorial Optimization
summary: Large Language Models have recently emerged as a promising paradigm for automated heuristic design for NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems. Despite this progress, existing LLM-based methods typically rely on monolithic workflows constrained by rigid templates, thereby restricting memory-guided exploration and triggering premature convergence to local optima. To design an autonomous and collaborative architecture, we introduce HMACE, a Heterogeneous Multi-Agent Collaborative Evolution framework that reconceptualizes heuristic search as an organizational design problem. HMACE decomposes each evolutionary generation into an autonomous, role-specialized loop with four coordinated agents: a Proposer for strategy exploration, a Generator for executable heuristic synthesis, an Evaluator for empirical assessment, and a Reflector for archive-backed memory update. By coupling behavior-aware retrieval, lightweight candidate filtering, and fitness-grounded archive updates, HMACE guides the search toward diverse and promising heuristic behaviors while avoiding redundant evaluations. Extensive evaluations on representative COPs, including TSP, Online BPP, MKP, and PFSP, show that HMACE achieves a favorable quality-efficiency trade-off compared to state-of-the-art single-agent and multi-agent baselines. In the matched LLM-driven reference comparison, HMACE achieves the lowest average gaps on TSP and Online BPP (0.464\% and 0.223\%, respectively), while requiring only 0.13M and 0.42M tokens for the two tasks, substantially fewer than the compared baselines.

AI.tldr: HMACE is a Heterogeneous Multi-Agent Collaborative Evolution framework that decomposes heuristic search into four specialized agents (Proposer, Generator, Evaluator, Reflector) for automated heuristic design, achieving superior quality-efficiency trade-offs on NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems compared to existing LLM-based methods.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based methods for automated heuristic design rely on monolithic workflows with rigid templates, which restrict memory-guided exploration and trigger premature convergence to local optima. The goal is to design an autonomous and collaborative architecture that overcomes these limitations.
AI.method: HMACE reconceptualizes heuristic search as an organizational design problem, decomposing each evolutionary generation into a role-specialized loop with four coordinated agents: Proposer (strategy exploration), Generator (executable heuristic synthesis), Evaluator (empirical assessment), and Reflector (archive-backed memory update). It also incorporates behavior-aware retrieval, lightweight candidate filtering, and fitness-grounded archive updates.
AI.result: Evaluated on TSP, Online BPP, MKP, and PFSP, HMACE achieves favorable quality-efficiency trade-offs vs. state-of-the-art baselines. In matched LLM-driven comparisons, it achieves lowest average gaps on TSP (0.464%) and Online BPP (0.223%) while requiring only 0.13M and 0.42M tokens respectively.
AI.conclusion: HMACE demonstrates that a heterogeneous multi-agent collaborative architecture with role specialization and memory-guided search can effectively balance solution quality and computational efficiency for automated heuristic design in combinatorial optimization.

title: MEMOREPAIR: Barrier-First Cascade Repair in Agentic Memory
summary: Agentic memory evolves across tasks into durable derived artifacts: summaries, cached outputs, embeddings, learned skills, and executable tool procedures. When a source artifact is deleted, corrected, or invalidated by tool or API migration, descendants derived from that source can remain visible and steer future actions with stale support. We formalize this failure mode as the cascade update problem, where repair targets the visible derived state of the memory store. We present MemoRepair, a barrier-first cascade-repair contract for agentic memory. A repair event induces a controlled transition from invalidated descendant state to validated successor state: affected descendants are withdrawn before repair, successors are constructed from retained support and staged repaired predecessors under the current interface, and republication is restricted to validated predecessor-closed successors. This contract induces a scalarized repair-selection problem for a fixed repair-cost tradeoff. We show that the induced publication problem reduces to maximum-weight predecessor closure and can be solved exactly by a single s-t min-cut. Experiments on ToolBench and MemoryArena show that, with complete influence provenance, MemoRepair reduces invalidated-memory exposure from 69.8-94.3% under systems without cascade repair to 0%. Compared with exhaustive Repair all, it recovers 91.1-94.3% of validated successors while reducing normalized repair-operator cost from 1.00 to 0.57-0.76.

AI.tldr: MemoRepair introduces a cascade-update contract for agentic memory that systematically invalidates and replaces derived artifacts when source dependencies change, achieving 0% invalidated-memory exposure with 57-76% of full-repair cost.
AI.motivation: When source artifacts in agentic memory are deleted, corrected, or invalidated, their descendants (summaries, embeddings, learned skills, etc.) remain visible and can steer future actions with stale support, creating a failure mode the authors formalize as the cascade update problem.
AI.method: MemoRepair is a barrier-first cascade-repair contract with three phases: (1) withdrawal of affected descendants, (2) construction of successors from retained support and staged repaired predecessors under the current interface, and (3) restriction of republication to validated predecessor-closed successors. The publication subproblem reduces to maximum-weight predecessor closure solved by a single s-t min-cut.
AI.result: On ToolBench and MemoryArena, MemoRepair reduces invalidated-memory exposure from 69.8-94.3% to 0%. Compared to exhaustive Repair-all, it recovers 91.1-94.3% of validated successors while reducing normalized repair-operator cost from 1.00 to 0.57-0.76.
AI.conclusion: The cascade update problem is tractable under complete influence provenance; MemoRepair's predecessor-closure formulation enables optimal, cost-efficient repair of derived agentic memory artifacts.

title: EnvSimBench: A Benchmark for Evaluating and Improving LLM-Based Environment Simulation
summary: Scalable AI agents training relies on interactive environments that faithfully simulate the consequences of agent actions. Manually crafted environments are expensive to build, brittle to extend, and fundamentally limited in diversity. A promising direction is to replace manually crafted environments with LLM-simulated counterparts. However, this paradigm hinges on an unexamined core assumption: LLMs can accurately simulate environmental feedback. In practice, LLM-simulated environments suffer from hallucinations, logical inconsistencies, and silent state drift failures that corrupt agent reward signals and compound the construction costs that the paradigm was designed to eliminate. To address this gap, we propose EnvSimBench with four contributions: 1) We provide the first formal definition and operationalization of Environment Simulation Ability (EnvSim Ability) as a quantifiable research objective. 2) We construct EnvSimBench, a rigorous benchmark covering 400 samples across 167 diverse environments, equipped with verifiable labels and fine-grained difficulty stratification along three axes. 3) Systematic evaluations reveal that all state-of-the-art language models suffer from a universal state change cliff: they achieve near-perfect accuracy on tasks when the environment state remains invariant, yet fail catastrophically when multiple states need simultaneous updates. This finding exposes EnvSim Ability as a critical yet largely unaddressed capability gap. 4) We design a constraint-driven simulation pipeline that substantially reduces hallucination, boosts environment synthesis yield by 6.8%, and cuts costs by over 90%. Overall, EnvSimBench serves as both a diagnostic framework and a practical optimization path for reliable LLM-based environment simulation, establishing a foundation for scalable agent training. Code and data are available at https://github.com/cookieApril/EnvSimBench

AI.tldr: EnvSimBench is a benchmark and framework for evaluating and improving LLMs' ability to accurately simulate interactive environments for AI agent training. It formalizes Environment Simulation Ability, reveals a universal "state change cliff" where LLMs fail on multi-state updates, and proposes a constraint-driven pipeline that reduces hallucinations, boosts synthesis yield by 6.8%, and cuts costs by over 90%.
AI.motivation: Manually crafted environments for agent training are expensive, brittle, and limited in diversity. While LLM-simulated environments offer a promising alternative, they suffer from hallucinations, logical inconsistencies, and silent state drift that corrupt reward signals and compound costs. There is no existing framework to quantify this capability gap.
AI.method: 1) Formal definition and operationalization of Environment Simulation Ability (EnvSim Ability). 2) Construction of EnvSimBench with 400 samples across 167 environments, verifiable labels, and fine-grained difficulty stratification along three axes. 3) Systematic evaluation of state-of-the-art LLMs. 4) Design of a constraint-driven simulation pipeline for improvement.
AI.result: All SOTA language models exhibit a universal "state change cliff": near-perfect accuracy on invariant state tasks but catastrophic failure when multiple states need simultaneous updates. The constraint-driven pipeline reduces hallucination, boosts synthesis yield by 6.8%, and cuts costs by over 90%.
AI.conclusion: EnvSimAbility is a critical yet largely unaddressed capability gap in LLMs. EnvSimBench serves as both a diagnostic framework and a practical optimization path toward reliable LLM-based environment simulation, establishing a foundation for scalable agent training.

title: Can Agents Price a Reaction? Evaluating LLMs on Chemical Cost Reasoning
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have become increasingly capable as tool-using agents, with benchmarks spanning diverse general agentic tasks. Yet rigorous evaluation of scientific tool use remains limited. In chemistry, recent agents can plan syntheses and invoke domain-specific tools, but evaluations often rely on curated demonstrations, expert assessment, or LLM-as-judge scoring rather than exact, judge-free ground truth. We address this gap with chemical procurement cost estimation, a practical task in which an agent must ground chemical identities, retrieve supplier quotes, select valid purchasable packs, normalize quantities, and compute cost from a reaction description. We introduce ChemCost, a benchmark of 1,427 evaluable reactions grounded to a frozen pricing snapshot covering 2,261 chemicals and 230,775 supplier quotes, supporting scalar scoring and stage-level diagnosis of grounding, retrieval, procurement, and arithmetic failures. To evaluate robustness, we further construct controlled noise-injected views that perturb chemical aliases, quantity expressions, missing fields, and input formatting. Experiments with frontier, open-weight, and chemistry-specialized LLM agents show that tool access is necessary but insufficient for solving the task. The strongest agents reach only 50.6% accuracy within 25% relative error on clean inputs and degrade substantially with realistic noise. Stage-level analysis further shows that failures arise from brittle parsing, ineffective evidence integration, invalid pack selection, and non-convergent tool use.

AI.tldr: ChemCost is a benchmark of 1,427 chemistry reactions with pricing data that evaluates LLM agents on cost estimation, finding that even the best agents achieve only 50.6% accuracy within 25% error and degrade under realistic noise due to brittle parsing, poor evidence integration, and ineffective tool use.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of scientific tool use by LLMs rely on curated demonstrations, expert assessment, or LLM-as-judge scoring rather than exact, judge-free ground truth, creating a gap for rigorous, objective evaluation of agents in chemistry tasks.
AI.method: ChemCost benchmark with 1,427 evaluable reactions grounded to a frozen pricing snapshot (2,261 chemicals, 230,775 supplier quotes); controlled noise-injected views perturbing chemical aliases, quantity expressions, missing fields, and input formatting; stage-level diagnostic analysis of grounding, retrieval, procurement, and arithmetic failures.
AI.result: Strongest agents reach only 50.6% accuracy within 25% relative error on clean inputs; performance degrades substantially with realistic noise; tool access is necessary but insufficient for solving the task.
AI.conclusion: Failures arise from brittle parsing, ineffective evidence integration, invalid pack selection, and non-convergent tool use, highlighting fundamental limitations in current LLM agents for scientific tool-using tasks.

title: Structured Role-Aware Policy Optimization for Multimodal Reasoning
summary: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR), especially with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), has shown strong potential for improving the reasoning capabilities of large vision-language models (LVLMs). However, in multimodal reasoning, final-answer rewards are typically assigned at the sequence level and do not distinguish the functional roles of different tokens, making it difficult to determine whether a correct answer is supported by task-relevant visual evidence. In this paper, we revisit multimodal RLVR from the perspective of role-aware token-level credit assignment, where structured responses are decomposed into perception tokens for extracting visual evidence and reasoning tokens for deriving answers from that evidence. Based on this perspective, we propose Structured Role-aware Policy Optimization (SRPO), which refines the sequence-level GRPO advantage into role-aware token-level advantages without changing the reward function. Specifically, SRPO assigns role-specific credit by using self-distilled on-policy contrasts: perception tokens are emphasized according to their visual dependency under original versus corrupted visual inputs, while reasoning tokens are emphasized according to their consistency with the generated perception. These role-specific signals are further unified through a shared trajectory-level baseline, yielding positive token weights that adjust relative update magnitudes while preserving the original GRPO reward and optimization direction, without requiring external reward models or separate teachers. Experiments across diverse multimodal reasoning benchmarks show that SRPO improves evidence-grounded reasoning, highlighting the importance of moving beyond uniform sequence-level credit toward role-aware optimization for reliable multimodal reasoning.

AI.tldr: SRPO improves multimodal reasoning in LVLMs by assigning role-aware token-level credit (perception vs. reasoning tokens) within GRPO, using self-distilled contrasts to replace sequence-level rewards, boosting evidence-grounded reasoning without external models.
AI.motivation: Standard RLVR/GRPO assigns sequence-level final-answer rewards that fail to distinguish token roles (perception vs. reasoning), making it unclear if a correct answer is backed by relevant visual evidence. This undermines reliable multimodal reasoning.
AI.method: SRPO decomposes structured responses into perception tokens (extracting visual evidence) and reasoning tokens (deriving answers). It refines GRPO's sequence-level advantage into role-aware token-level advantages using self-distilled on-policy contrasts: perception tokens weighted by visual dependency under corrupted vs. original inputs; reasoning tokens weighted by consistency with generated perception. These are unified via a shared trajectory-level baseline, yielding positive token weights that adjust update magnitudes while preserving GRPO's reward and optimization direction.
AI.result: Across diverse multimodal reasoning benchmarks, SRPO improves evidence-grounded reasoning compared to standard sequence-level GRPO, demonstrating the effectiveness of role-aware credit assignment.
AI.conclusion: Moving beyond uniform sequence-level credit toward role-aware optimization is crucial for reliable multimodal reasoning, and SRPO provides an effective approach that requires no external reward models or separate teachers.

title: Signal Reshaping for GRPO in Weak-Feedback Agentic Code Repair
summary: Code-agent RL often receives weak feedback: rollout-time signals are reliable and executable, but capture only necessary or surface conditions for task success rather than the target semantic predicate. Using agentic compile-fix as the setting, we study signal reshaping for standard GRPO under such feedback. Our central claim is that GRPO's within-group comparison is meaningful only after three kinds of signals are reshaped: outcome rewards recover semantic ranking, process signals localize intra-trajectory credit, and rollouts from the same prompt remain execution-comparable. We operationalize these conditions with a minimal signal-reshaping construction that leaves GRPO's group-normalized advantage construction unchanged: compile-and-semantic layered rewards reshape trajectory ranking, step-level process scores outside group reward normalization reshape within-trajectory update strength, and failure-cause-aware rollout governance reshapes within-group comparability. Experiments show a clear end-to-end gain: full signal-reshaped GRPO improves strict compile-and-semantic accuracy from the base model's zero-shot $0.385$ to $0.535$. Controlled comparisons further explain the source of this gain: binary rewards remove the compile-only middle tier and degrade trajectory control; on top of layered rewards, process-score weighting further improves accuracy from $0.48$ to $0.53$ and reduces average evaluation steps from $23.50$ to $17.02$. As a boundary comparison, privileged-prompt token-level distillation mainly optimizes local distributional alignment; in long tool-use trajectories, this signal is diluted by non-critical tokens and cannot replace outcome semantics, process credit, or within-group comparability.

AI.tldr: This paper studies signal reshaping for GRPO in code-agent RL (compile-fix setting), proposing three conditions for meaningful within-group comparison: outcome rewards that capture semantic ranking, process signals for intra-trajectory credit, and execution-comparable rollouts. A minimal reshaping construction (compile-and-semantic layered rewards, step-level process scores, failure-cause-aware governance) improves accuracy from 0.385 to 0.535 and reduces evaluation steps.
AI.motivation: Code-agent RL often uses weak feedback (rollout-time signals) that capture only surface conditions rather than the true semantic predicate. The authors aim to reshape these signals to make GRPO's within-group comparison meaningful and improve task success in agentic compile-fix settings.
AI.method: Three signal-reshaping conditions are operationalized: (1) compile-and-semantic layered rewards for trajectory ranking, (2) step-level process scores outside group reward normalization for within-trajectory update strength, and (3) failure-cause-aware rollout governance for within-group comparability. These are applied to standard GRPO without changing its group-normalized advantage construction.
AI.result: Full signal-reshaped GRPO improves strict compile-and-semantic accuracy from 0.385 to 0.535. Layered rewards improve accuracy from 0.48 to 0.53; process-score weighting further reduces evaluation steps from 23.50 to 17.02. Binary rewards degrade performance by removing the compile-only middle tier.
AI.conclusion: GRPO's within-group comparison is meaningful only when outcome semantics, process credit, and within-group comparability are properly reshaped. Privileged token-level distillation cannot replace these components in long tool-use trajectories due to token dilution.

title: SOM: Structured Opponent Modeling for LLM-based Agents via Structural Causal Model
summary: Accurately predicting opponents' behavior from interactions is a fundamental capability for large language model (LLM)-based agents in multi-agent and game-theoretic environments. Existing approaches often entangle opponent modeling with prediction, relying on implicit contextual reasoning and limiting adaptability in dynamic interactions. To this end, we propose Structured Opponent Modeling (SOM), a two-stage opponent modeling framework that distinctly separates opponent model construction and opponent prediction. At the construction stage, SOM employs a Structural Causal Model (SCM), a graph-based formalism for representing dependencies among variables, to capture directed links between opponents' observations and actions, yielding an explicit and structured opponent representation. At the prediction stage, the LLM performs structured reasoning along clear pathways derived from the SCM, improving both prediction accuracy and stability. Extensive experiments on diverse multi-agent benchmarks demonstrate that SOM consistently outperforms state-of-the-art LLM-based reasoning baselines, enabling more accurate and adaptable strategic decision-making in complex and dynamic multi-agent interactions.

AI.tldr: SOM is a two-stage opponent modeling framework that separates opponent model construction (using Structural Causal Models) from opponent prediction (via structured LLM reasoning), outperforming existing LLM-based baselines in multi-agent benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based opponent modeling approaches entangle model construction with prediction, relying on implicit contextual reasoning, which limits adaptability in dynamic multi-agent interactions.
AI.method: Two-stage framework: (1) Construction stage uses Structural Causal Models (SCM) to capture directed links between opponents' observations and actions; (2) Prediction stage uses the SCM-derived causal pathways to guide LLM structured reasoning for accurate opponent prediction.
AI.result: Consistently outperforms state-of-the-art LLM-based reasoning baselines across diverse multi-agent benchmarks, improving prediction accuracy, stability, and strategic decision-making adaptability.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling opponent model construction from prediction via explicit causal graphs enables more accurate and adaptable opponent modeling in complex, dynamic multi-agent settings.

title: When Stored Evidence Stops Being Usable: Scale-Conditioned Evaluation of Agent Memory
summary: Memory-agent evaluations report fixed-snapshot accuracy or retrieval quality, but these scores do not show whether evidence remains usable as irrelevant sessions (sessions not annotated as task-relevant evidence for the query) accumulate. We present a scale-conditioned evaluation protocol for agent memory under evidence-preserving growth: for each query, task evidence is held fixed while irrelevant sessions are added. The protocol logs agent--memory trajectories and reports four diagnostics: budget-compliant reliability, tail memory-call burden, failure-regime decomposition, and the usable-scale boundary where reliability falls below the target. Applied to LongMemEval and LoCoMo across flat, planar, and hierarchical memory interfaces, the protocol shows reliability loss is not a single phenomenon. On LongMemEval, HippoRAG stays within the two-call budget but loses 16--20 percentage points in budget-compliant reliability as irrelevant sessions are added; LiCoMemory's observed failures depend strongly on the agent, with Qwen3-8B exceeding the budget while Qwen3-32B and Qwen3-235B remain reliable in the tested range. The result supports a framework for making scalable-memory claims conditional on agent, interface, scale range, and interaction budget.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a scale-conditioned evaluation protocol for agent memory that holds task evidence fixed while adding irrelevant sessions, reporting four diagnostics: budget-compliant reliability, tail memory-call burden, failure-regime decomposition, and usable-scale boundary. Applied to LongMemEval and LoCoMo, it reveals that reliability loss varies by agent, interface, and scale, and supports making scalable-memory claims conditional on these factors.
AI.motivation: Existing memory-agent evaluations report fixed-snapshot accuracy or retrieval quality, but fail to assess whether evidence remains usable as irrelevant sessions accumulate over time.
AI.method: A scale-conditioned evaluation protocol for agent memory under evidence-preserving growth: task evidence is held fixed while irrelevant sessions are added; it logs agent–memory trajectories and reports four diagnostics (budget-compliant reliability, tail memory-call burden, failure-regime decomposition, usable-scale boundary).
AI.result: Applied to LongMemEval and LoCoMo across flat, planar, and hierarchical memory interfaces. HippoRAG stays within the two-call budget but loses 16–20 percentage points in reliability; LiCoMemory's failures depend strongly on the agent—Qwen3-8B exceeds the budget, while Qwen3-32B and Qwen3-235B remain reliable.
AI.conclusion: Reliability loss is not a single phenomenon; scalable-memory claims should be made conditional on agent, interface, scale range, and interaction budget.

title: Implicit Compression Regularization: Concise Reasoning via Internal Shorter Distributions in RL Post-Training
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards improves LLM reasoning but often induces overthinking, where models generate unnecessarily long reasoning traces. Existing methods mainly rely on length penalties or early-exit strategies; however, the former may degrade accuracy and induce underthinking, whereas the latter assumes that substantial portions of reasoning traces can be safely truncated. To obtain a compression signal without these limitations, we revisit the training dynamics of existing compression methods. We observe that the length--accuracy correlation is initially negative but continually increases during compression, indicating that shorter responses are initially more likely to be correct but gradually lose this property as the policy moves toward underthinking. Based on this observation, we formalize overthinking: a negative correlation indicates an overthinking regime, while a positive one indicates underthinking. When overthinking, the shortest correct responses are shorter than the group-average response length in expectation, making them natural compression targets already present in on-policy rollouts. We therefore propose \emph{Implicit Compression Regularization} (ICR), an on-policy regularization method whose compression signal comes from a virtual shorter distribution induced by the shortest correct responses in rollout groups, guiding the policy toward concise yet correct trajectories. Training dynamics show that ICR maintains a better length--accuracy correlation during compression, indicating that short responses remain better aligned with correctness instead of drifting toward underthinking. Experiments on three reasoning backbones and multiple mathematical and knowledge-intensive benchmarks show that ICR consistently shortens responses while preserving or improving accuracy, achieving a stronger accuracy--length Pareto frontier.

AI.tldr: ICR is an on-policy regularization method that uses shortest correct responses in rollout groups as implicit compression targets to reduce overthinking in LLM reasoning without the drawbacks of length penalties or early-exit strategies.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for reducing overthinking in LLM reasoning (length penalties, early-exit) degrade accuracy, induce underthinking, or assume safe truncation of reasoning traces. A better compression signal is needed that avoids these limitations.
AI.method: ICR observes the length-accuracy correlation dynamics: negative correlation = overthinking, positive = underthinking. It uses the shortest correct responses in on-policy rollout groups as virtual shorter distribution targets to regularize the policy toward concise yet correct trajectories.
AI.result: ICR maintains a better length-accuracy correlation during compression (short responses stay aligned with correctness). It consistently shortens responses while preserving/improving accuracy across three reasoning backbones and multiple math/knowledge benchmarks, achieving a stronger accuracy-length Pareto frontier.
AI.conclusion: Implicit Compression Regularization effectively mitigates overthinking without causing underthinking or accuracy degradation, offering a superior trade-off between response length and reasoning accuracy.

title: Discovering Ordinary Differential Equations with LLM-Based Qualitative and Quantitative Evaluation
summary: Discovering governing differential equations from observational data is a fundamental challenge in scientific machine learning. Existing symbolic regression approaches rely primarily on quantitative metrics; however, real-world differential equation modeling also requires incorporating domain knowledge to ensure physical plausibility. To address this gap, we propose DoLQ, a method for discovering ordinary differential equations with LLM-based qualitative and quantitative evaluation. DoLQ employs a multi-agent architecture: a Sampler Agent proposes dynamic system candidates, a Parameter Optimizer refines equations for accuracy, and a Scientist Agent leverages an LLM to conduct both qualitative and quantitative evaluations and synthesize their results to iteratively guide the search. Experiments on multi-dimensional ordinary differential equation benchmarks demonstrate that DoLQ achieves superior performance compared to existing methods, not only attaining higher success rates but also more accurately recovering the correct symbolic terms of ground truth equations. Our code is available at https://github.com/Bon99yun/DoLQ.

AI.tldr: DoLQ is a multi-agent LLM-based method for discovering governing differential equations from observational data, combining qualitative (domain knowledge) and quantitative evaluations to iteratively guide symbolic regression, achieving superior performance on ODE benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing symbolic regression approaches rely primarily on quantitative metrics, but real-world differential equation modeling also requires incorporating domain knowledge to ensure physical plausibility.
AI.method: DoLQ employs a multi-agent architecture with three agents: a Sampler Agent (proposes dynamic system candidates), a Parameter Optimizer (refines equations for accuracy), and a Scientist Agent (uses an LLM for qualitative and quantitative evaluations, synthesizing results to iteratively guide search).
AI.result: Experiments on multi-dimensional ODE benchmarks show DoLQ achieves higher success rates and more accurately recovers correct symbolic terms of ground truth equations compared to existing methods.
AI.conclusion: DoLQ effectively bridges the gap between quantitative symbolic regression and qualitative domain knowledge integration for ODE discovery, demonstrating superior performance.

title: Tools as Continuous Flow for Evolving Agentic Reasoning
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in orchestrating tools for reasoning tasks. However, existing methods rely on a step-wise paradigm that lacks a global perspective, which causes error accumulation over long horizons and restricts generalization to unseen tools. To overcome these limitations, we propose Tools as Continuous Flow for Evolving Agentic Reasoning (FlowAgent), which reconceptualizes tool chaining as continuous trajectory generation within a semantic space. To systematically evaluate this paradigm, we introduce the first plan-level closed-loop benchmark dedicated to plan-level agentic reasoning in dynamic real-world environments. Specifically, the proposed FlowAgent leverages conditional flow matching to generate continuous latent trajectories, providing a global planning perspective to ensure coherent and robust tool execution. Theoretically, we establish formal bounds on utility convergence and prove that our continuous formulation fundamentally guarantees robust generalization and error attenuation. Empirical evaluations show that FlowAgent achieves superior robustness and adaptability in long-horizon reasoning tasks.

AI.tldr: FlowAgent reimagines tool chaining as continuous trajectory generation in semantic space using conditional flow matching, achieving robust and generalizable long-horizon agentic reasoning with theoretical guarantees on error attenuation and utility convergence.
AI.motivation: Existing step-wise LLM tool orchestration methods lack a global perspective, causing error accumulation over long horizons and poor generalization to unseen tools.
AI.method: Proposes FlowAgent which uses conditional flow matching to generate continuous latent trajectories for tool chaining, reconceptualizing discrete tool calls as continuous flow in semantic space. Also introduces a plan-level closed-loop benchmark for dynamic real-world evaluation.
AI.result: Empirically demonstrates superior robustness and adaptability in long-horizon reasoning tasks. Theoretically establishes formal bounds on utility convergence and proves continuous formulation guarantees robust generalization and error attenuation.
AI.conclusion: The continuous trajectory paradigm effectively overcomes error accumulation and generalization limitations of step-wise tool reasoning, providing a principled framework for agentic reasoning.

title: Confidence-Aware Alignment Makes Reasoning LLMs More Reliable
summary: Large reasoning models often reach correct answers through flawed intermediate steps, creating a gap between final accuracy and reasoning reliability. Existing alignment strategies address this with external verifiers or massive sampling, limiting scalability. In this work, we introduce CASPO (Confidence-Aware Step-wise Preference Optimization), a framework that aligns token-level confidence with step-wise logical correctness through iterative Direct Preference Optimization, without training a separate reward model. During inference, we propose Confidence-aware Thought (CaT), which leverages this calibrated confidence to dynamically prune uncertain reasoning branches with negligible O(V) latency. Experiments across ten benchmarks and multiple model families show that CASPO consistently improves reasoning reliability and inference efficiency. CASPO scales to Qwen3-8B-Base and surpasses tree-search baselines on AIME'24 and AIME'25 without using reward-model data. We also release a step-wise dataset with confidence annotations to support fine-grained analysis of reasoning reliability. Code is available at https://github.com/Thecommonirin/CASPO.

AI.tldr: CASPO aligns token-level confidence with step-wise logical correctness via iterative DPO without a separate reward model, and CaT uses calibrated confidence for pruning uncertain reasoning branches at inference, improving both reasoning reliability and efficiency across benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Large reasoning models often produce correct answers through flawed intermediate steps, creating a gap between final accuracy and reasoning reliability. Existing alignment strategies rely on external verifiers or massive sampling, which limits scalability.
AI.method: CASPO uses iterative Direct Preference Optimization to align token-level confidence with step-wise logical correctness without training a separate reward model. During inference, Confidence-aware Thought (CaT) leverages calibrated confidence to dynamically prune uncertain reasoning branches with low latency.
AI.result: CASPO consistently improves reasoning reliability and inference efficiency across ten benchmarks and multiple model families. It scales to Qwen3-8B-Base and surpasses tree-search baselines on AIME'24 and AIME'25 without reward-model data.
